title: Redox state of subducted sediments controls porphyry copper mineralization along the Tethyan belt

paper_content.abstract: The Tethyan orogenic belt hosts numerous world-class porphyry copper deposits, with most forming during the Cenozoic continental collision and fewer during earlier Mesozoic subduction. To understand this pattern, we integrate redox indicators from detrital zircon grains with constraints from sedimentary geology and granite geochemistry during these times. Our analysis reveals a major shift from reduced magmas forming during the Mesozoic to more oxidized intrusive systems in the Cenozoic. Here we show that subduction of organic-rich, reduced marine sediments in the Mesozoic suppressed the oxidation state of arc magmas, locking chalcophile elements in the lower crust and inhibiting the formation of porphyry Cu deposits. In contrast, the subduction of more oxidized continental sediments during Cenozoic collision elevated the mantle’s oxidation state, releasing stored copper to melts that form porphyry deposits. These findings highlight the critical role of redox state of subducted sediments and tectonic history in shaping the distribution of porphyry mineralization along the Tethyan belt.
paper_content.introduction:
The Tethyan orogenic belt, extending for 12,000 km from the Pyrenees through the Alps and the Turkish–Iranian plateau, across Pakistan and the Himalayan–Tibetan Plateau, and into the Indochina Peninsula (Fig. 1a), is one of the world’s most important porphyry Cu belts1–4. This orogen formed through successive stages of continental breakup, ocean basin formation, and eventual collision between Gondwana-derived continents and Eurasia (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Material). The Tethys realm can be divided chronologically into the Proto-, Paleo-, and Neo-Tethys oceans, formed during the Early Paleozoic, Late Paleozoic, and Mesozoic, respectively5. Of particular interest is the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which opened in the Early Permian and underwent protracted subduction during the Mesozoic, culminating in extensive Cenozoic continental collisions that led to the formation of porphyry Cu deposits in regions such as the Gangdese and Yulong belts (Tibet), the Kerman belt (Iran), and the Anatolides belt (Turkey)1,2,5–8 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Material).

Despite a long Mesozoic subduction history, significantly fewer and smaller porphyry Cu deposits formed during subduction-related magmatism than during Cenozoic collisional or post-collisional magmatic stages in the Tethyan belt (Figs. 1b, 2c). The reason for this disparity remains elusive. A key control on porphyry copper formation is the oxidation state of the magmatic system, i.e., magmatic oxygen fugacity, commonly expressed as ΔFMQ (the log of oxygen fugacity relative to the fayalite–magnetite–quartz buffer). Oxidized arc magmas (ΔFMQ ≈ +1 to +2) favor the mobilization of chalcophile elements, enabling their transport to the upper crust9,10. Detrital zircon provides a valuable record of magmatic redox conditions over geologic timescales. Global geological events–particularly oceanic anoxic events and seawater incursion events–can influence the geochemical composition of subducted sediments11,12, altering mantle wedge oxygen fugacity and affecting porphyry mineralization potential.

Here, we apply a multidisciplinary approach to track the oxygen fugacity evolution of Tethyan magmas from the Early Jurassic to the Miocene. Using the novel zircon oxybarometer, we reconstruct ΔFMQ through time and integrate these data with sedimentary rocks, global sea-level and temperature changes, whole-rock geochemical data, and the timing of major geological events. Our findings illuminate the mechanisms responsible for redox variations in the mantle wedge and their implications for subduction- vs. collision-related porphyry Cu deposits.
paper_content.results:
Redox variation from Mesozoic to Cenozoic
Detrital zircon oxybarometry reveals an overall increase in ΔFMQ from the Early Jurassic through the Miocene in the Tethyan belt (Fig. 2d). Although data density during the Jurassic to Early Cretaceous is relatively low and thus more variable, Mesozoic ΔFMQ values are predominantly below +1. By contrast, Cenozoic ΔFMQ values commonly exceed +1, consistent with a transition to more oxidized magmatic conditions (Fig. 2d). The V/Sc ratios are also widely used as a redox proxy in igneous rocks, with higher ratios indicating more oxidized magmas19. The oxidation states of mid-oceanic ridge basalts (MORBs) close to ΔFMQ ~ 0 have V/Sc ratios of 6.74 ± 1.11. We compiled V/Sc data from Tethyan magmatic rocks (Supplementary Data 3). The results shows the lower V/Sc ratios of Mesozoic rocks (median = 6.9, n = 631) are like MORBs, while the Cenozoic rocks have higher V/Sc ratios (median = 8.4, n = 786) (Supplementary Fig. 2). The V/Sc results are consistent with our zircon ΔFMQ results, both indicated the Cenozoic ƒO2 is higher than the Mesozoic. Under low ƒO2, sulfur tends to form sulfides. The chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Au) have high partition coefficients between sulfide and silicate melts10. As a result, the chalcophile elements were sequestered in the lower crust via sulfide accumulation under low ƒO2, resulting in rare mineralization in the upper crust9,10,20. This process parallels the anoxic conditions inferred for the Paleo-Tethys Ocean basin during the Permian when the basin was in a restricted environment near the equator21,22. The correlation between redox state and porphyry Cu deposit frequency (Fig. 2c, d) supports redox-driven control over the spatiotemporal distribution of Tethyan porphyry Cu mineralization.
paper_content.methods:
Materials
The zircon age and trace elements are compiled from the global detrital zircon database68 and our newly acquired data in Tibet. The complete database includes 13981 detrital zircons (see details in Supplementary Data 2).

Zircon U–Pb dating and trace element analyses
Zircon grains were separated from two rivers in Tibet and mounted in epoxy resin for age and trace element determinations. Zircon U–Pb dating and trace element analyses were conducted simultaneously by laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA–ICP–MS) in the Mineral and Fluid Inclusion Microanalysis Laboratory, Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing, China. The NWR193UC laser ablation system (Elemental Scientific Lasers, USA) was equipped with a Coherent Excistar 200 excimer laser and a two-volume ablation cell. The laser ablation system was coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP–MS instrument (Agilent, USA). Zircons were mounted in epoxy resin discs, polished to expose grain interiors, cleaned ultrasonically in ultrapure water, and then cleaned again before analysis using analytical-grade methanol. Pre-ablation was conducted before each spot analysis using five laser shots (~0.3 μm in depth) to remove potential surface contamination. The analyses used a 30 μm laser beam diameter with a laser frequency of 8 Hz and fluence of 2 J/cm2. The Iolite software package was used for data reduction69. Zircons 91500 and GJ-1 were the primary and secondary reference materials, respectively. The exponential function was used to correct for down-hole fractionation70. NIST 610 and 91Zr were used to calibrate the trace element concentrations as an external reference material and internal standard, respectively. Zircon age and trace element data are listed in Supplementary Data 2.

Calculation of oxygen fugacity
Data points outside the Tethys domain were excluded. Zircon ages younger than 200 Ma are used for the following discussion to minimize the influence of the Paleo-Tethys Oceanic subduction because the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean occurred in the Late Permian–Late Triassic5. Zircons with a Th/U ratio of <0.1 were used to exclude metamorphic zircon71. Moreover, zircons derived from S-type granites were screened out using zircon P and REE contents72. After screening, 3010 zircon grains were used for reconstructing the Tethyan oxygen fugacity variation (Supplementary Data 2). The novel magmatic oxybarometer using ratios of Ce, U, and Ti in zircon is independent of temperature and pressure, with a standard error of ±0.6 log unit ƒO2 73. The ΔFMQ values can be calculated by the equation:

ΔFMQ = 3.998 (±0.124) × log[Ce / (U × T)] + 2.284 (±0.101) (1)

where Ui denotes age-corrected initial U content73. The ΔFMQ values are plotted as binned averages (bin size = 5 Myr).

Monte Carlo isotopic simulation
The Sr-Nd concentrations and isotopic ratios of the sediment–depleted mantle mixture can be calculated using the following equations:

Cx = Cs × F + Cm × (1 − F) (2)

Rx = Rs × F × Cs / Cx + Rm × (1 − F) × Cm / Cx (3)

where x is Sr or Nd, Cx, Cs, and Cm are element concentrations of x after mixing, sediment, and depleted mantle, respectively. Rx, Rs, and Rm are isotopic ratios of x after mixing, sediment, and depleted mantle, respectively, and F is the proportion of sediment-derived melt.

To obtain as many as possible mixture scenarios, random two pelagic or terrigenous sediments were selected and mixed to create a new pelagic or terrigenous sediment end-member. Then the new sediment end-member was mixed with the depleted mantle in random proportions. 30,000 pelagic sediment–mantle mixtures and 30,000 terrigenous sediment–mantle mixtures were generated using this method. The simulation results are shown in Fig. 4c, d.

Data availability
The data that support the findings of this study are available at Figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28424204).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript "Types of Subducted Material Controlling Tethyan Porphyry Copper Mineralization" presents a compelling
multidisciplinary investigation of redox evolution in the Tethyan orogenic belt and its critical role in porphyry copper
mineralization. By innovatively integrating detrital zircon oxybarmetry, geochemical analyses, stratigraphic constraints, and
global geological events, the authors establish a robust model linking subducted sediment redox states to porphyry copper
formation. This work successfully addresses the long-standing enigma of porphyry copper scarcity in the Tethyan belt. The
methodology is rigorous and the writing is clear. I recommend publication in Nature Communication after addressing the
following improvements.
1. In this manuscript, the authors proposed a model about the redox of subducted sediments controlling the Tethyan
porphyry Cu mineralization. Is the model a universal or regionally confined process? Is it applicable for other porphyry Cu
belts (e.g., Andes or Circum-Pacific arcs where porphyry deposits are primarily related to oceanic subduction)?
2. The authors focus narrowly on porphyry Cu deposits but does not explore implications for other redox-sensitive mineral
systems. If possible, provide a brief discussion on how redox-controlled processes in the Tethyan belt might inform
exploration for other deposit types globally.
3. The authors use zircon oxybarometry to estimate the variation of mantle wedge oxygen station from the Early Jurassic to
the Miocene, and further link this variation to subduction input of oxidized or reduced sediments. However, zircon is mainly
crystallized from felsic rocks that are not always generated via differentiation of mantle-derived magmas, but also can form
by partial melting of crustal materials. How to discriminate the detrital zircons in river sediments that were crystallized from
mantle- or crustal-derived melts? Moreover, magmatic rocks formed in different tectonic settings (e.g., arc vs. back-arc) may
also have distinct oxygen fugacity.
Other comments:
Line 73: This manuscript states the scarcity of Mesozoic subduction-related porphyry Cu deposits. What about the giant
Cretaceous porphyry Cu deposits in western Tethys (e.g., Romania, Serbia)?
Line 86–88: The discussion briefly mentions sulfur speciation (e.g., sulfides vs. sulfates) but does not elaborate on how this
affects metal mobility. Please include a more detailed discussion of sulfur speciation under different redox conditions and
how this influences the transport of chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Au).
Line 94-98: Please Elaborate on how sediments (e.g., organic-rich /oxidized) release reduced/oxidizing fluids during
subduction, affecting mantle wedge oxygen fugacity. If possible, provide redox reactions of subducted sediments in the
mantle source.
Line 217–236: What is the feasibility of zircon as an exploration tool? What is the difference between detrital zircons and
magmatic zircons as exploration implications, and their limitation?
Line 261: The detrital zircon oxybarometry method is applied here to trace the oxidation state evolution, while the results are
not cross-validated with other redox proxies (e.g., whole-rock V/Sc ratios) or zircons from magmatic rocks. Compare ∆FMQ
values with other redox indicators from Tethyan magmatic rocks (if available).
Figure 1: Add a scale bar in Figure 1a to facilitate distance estimation, even though it already includes latitude and
longitude.
Figure 2: Add text in Figure 2e to indicate the position of the Neo-Tethys Ocean and major continents.
Overall, this work represents a significant advancement in understanding metallogenic controls in collisional settings. Timely
publication would substantially benefit both academic research and mineral exploration communities. I look forward to
seeing the revised version.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript reads well. It is a good compilation of a large amount of data that confirms the paper published in Geology
by Richards and Sengor, 2017. Richards and Sengor showed that very few porphyry copper deposits formed during the
Paleo-Tethyan subduction due to organic-rich sediments subducted to the mantle, and that large deposits formed during
later Neo-Tethyan subduction. This manuscript provides the compilation of data related to the oxidation conditions of
magmas using the well-established method based on zircon trace-element composition, to confirm the shift in oxidation
conditions of igneous rocks, which reflects the source mantle.
This manuscript compiles types of sediments, the location and size of porphyry copper deposits, and data of host igneous
rocks (Supplementary text and data). In this sense, this manuscript provides a useful compilation of data from many porphyry
copper deposits along the Tethyan subduction zone. As mentioned, the data compilation confirms the conclusion of
Richards and Sengor, that there was a change in the oxidation conditions of the mantle and in the resultant magmas. The
manuscript also confirms other earlier publications, that oxidized magmas are conducive for porphyry copper mineralization
(e.g., Sillitoe, 2010; Shen et al., 2015; Loucks et al., 2024), and that subducted sediments influence the oxidation conditions
of the mantle and magmas (e.g., Wang et al., 2007; Evans, 2012),
The authors stress formation of large porphyry copper deposits during continental collision; the Neo-Tethys plate and
overlying sediments were subducted long after the closure of the Neo-Tethys, resulting in mantle metasomatization. The
continental collision and closure of the sea does not mean the end of subduction of oceanic plate. This has been well
illustrated by many tomographic images of subducted slabs below the Asian continent. Therefore, emphasizing the collision
stage for large porphyry copper deposits is misleading and confuses the issue.
The manuscript has stratigraphic columns of sediments, to provide support for the authors’ proposal, but the sections are
essentially similar to Figure 3 of the paper by Richards and Sengor. During the Mesozoic, sediments were reduced, such
that their subduction led to the mantle being reduced, resulting in the formation of reduced magmas.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Overall, this paper is well-written and presents a compelling narrative. The authors have compiled a comprehensive dataset
encompassing porphyry deposits, sedimentary rocks, global sea-level and temperature fluctuations, whole-rock
geochemistry, and major geological events. Their analysis reveals a strong correlation between redox variations and key
geological events in the Tethyan domain. Furthermore, they highlight the critical role of subducted sediment composition in
modulating redox conditions and controlling porphyry Cu deposit formation. Given the novelty and significance of these
findings, I believe this manuscript is well-suited for Nature Communications. I recommend minor revisions and suggest a few
points that could further strengthen the manuscript during the revision process:
1. Lines 173–174: The authors state that as mantle-derived ultrapotassic magmas ascend from ~56 km to ~15 km depth,
their ΔFMQ increases from +0.8 to +3.0, yet their ability to significantly oxidize magma in the lower crust remains limited.
However, in Lines 50–51, they also mention that oxidized arc magmas (ΔFMQ ≈ +1 to +2) promote the mobilization of
chalcophile elements, facilitating their transport to the upper crust. Considering the uncertainties in oxygen fugacity
calculations, FMQ +0.8 is nearly equivalent to FMQ +1. Additionally, oxygen fugacity estimations from detrital zircons
inherently carry errors. The authors could cite more recent references, as the oxygen fugacity of porphyry-related magmas is
generally considered to be higher in the deep source with high pressure.
2. The authors should briefly describe the zircon screening method and oxygen fugacity calculation in the main text. This
would provide better context for the Ce-U-Ti data and the europium anomaly-to-ytterbium ratio introduced later in the paper.
3. Figure 1b is highly informative, but the legends require clearer explanations to enhance readability and facilitate
interpretation.
4. Lines 182–183: The authors dismiss the autoxidation models of garnet and other minerals, arguing that these processes
do not apply to mantle source oxidation. However, in Figure 5b, they propose that sulfides were oxidized to sulfates in the
lower crust resulted from injection of oxidized ultrapotassic magmas. The authors need to give relative more detailed
introduction on how oxidizing agents are introduced during continental subduction, leading to high-fO2 mantle-derived
magmas that subsequently oxidize the juvenile lower crust.

This work successfully addresses the long-standing enigma of porphyry copper scarcity
in the Tethyan belt. The methodology is rigorous and the writing is clear. I recommend

1. In this manuscript, the authors proposed a model about the redox of subducted
sediments controlling the Tethyan porphyry Cu mineralization. Is the model a universal
or regionally confined process? Is it applicable for other porphyry Cu belts (e.g., Andes
or Circum-Pacific arcs where porphyry deposits are primarily related to oceanic
subduction)?
Response: We agree that clarifying the applicability of our model is critical. The Neo-
Tethyan Ocean is an east-west trend that has been near the equator for a long time and
has undergone oceanic opening, oceanic subduction, and closing processes. The Andes
or Circum-Pacific porphyry copper belt is related to the subduction of the (Paleo-)
Pacific Ocean, which has a south-north trend and is always in an open environment and
less prone to anoxia. In addition, the oxygen fugacity of the north-south trending Andes
arc may be latitude-dependent (Hu et al., 2024, NC). Therefore, the redox state is a
universal control for porphyry deposits, while the drivers of redox variations differ
regionally. Please see the new Lines 100–105.
2. The authors focus narrowly on porphyry Cu deposits but does not explore
implications for other redox-sensitive mineral systems. If possible, provide a brief
discussion on how redox-controlled processes in the Tethyan belt might inform
exploration for other deposit types globally.
Response: Thanks for the suggestion. We added a brief discussion on how redox-
controlled processes could guide exploration for W-Sn deposits (New Lines 251–256).
For example, high oxygen fugacity environments favor porphyry Cu mineralization,
whereas leads to massive precipitation of cassiterite and scheelite and hinders an
efficient transport of Sn-W elements from the magma source to the crust (Wu et al.,
2021, OGR). This expands the model’s relevance beyond porphyry Cu systems.
3. The authors use zircon oxybarometry to estimate the variation of mantle wedge
oxygen station from the Early Jurassic to the Miocene, and further link this variation to
subduction input of oxidized or reduced sediments. However, zircon is mainly
crystallized from felsic rocks that are not always generated via differentiation of
mantle-derived magmas, but also can form by partial melting of crustal materials. How
to discriminate the detrital zircons in river sediments that were crystallized from
mantle- or crustal-derived melts? Moreover, magmatic rocks formed in different
tectonic settings (e.g., arc vs. back-arc) may also have distinct oxygen fugacity.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical methodological concern. We
clarified in the Methods Section that detrital zircons were filtered using zircon P and
REE contents to exclude crustal sources (Zhu et al., 2020, EPSL). It is challenging to
identify the tectonic setting with detrital zircon. This manuscript focuses on the
statistical variation of oxygen fugacity with time.
Line 73: This manuscript states the scarcity of Mesozoic subduction-related porphyry
Cu deposits. What about the giant Cretaceous porphyry Cu deposits in western Tethys
(e.g., Romania, Serbia)?
Response: The oxidation state of the mantle wedge and related arc magmas in
subduction zones is heterogeneous due to the input of fluids and melts derived from the
subducted slab (Kelley and Cottrell, 2009, Science; Brounce et al., 2015, Geology;
Li et al., 2020, Geology). The magmatic zircon trace elements indicate the oxygen fugacity
from the Cretaceous porphyry deposits in Serbia are mainly ∆FMQ ≈ 0 to +1, with
minor ∆FMQ >1 (Klimentyeva et al., 2022, Geosciences). Overall, the magmatic
oxidation state in the Mesozoic is lower than Cenozoic.
Line 86–88: The discussion briefly mentions sulfur speciation (e.g., sulfides vs. sulfates)
but does not elaborate on how this affects metal mobility. Please include a more detailed
discussion of sulfur speciation under different redox conditions and
how this influences the transport of chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Au).
Response: The oxygen fugacity influences sulfur speciation. Under low oxygen
fugacity, the sulfur exits in the form of sulfide (S2-) and promotes precipitation of Cu2+
in the magma source, as a result, hindering the transport of chalcophile elements to the
shallow crust. In contrast, high oxygen fugacity causes sulfides (S2-) to oxidize to
sulfates (SO 2-), facilitating chalcophile elements' transport to the shallow crust (Sun et
al., 2015, OGR). We have added detail in the main text (New Lines 91–93).

subduction. The Paleo-Tethys and Neo-Tethys oceans are completely different entities.

deposits in the Tethyan belt formed during subduction of the Neo-Tethyan ocean basin

opposite; we identified that most porphyry deposits in the Tethyan belt are associated
with Cenozoic continental collision, while fewer are formed during subduction of the
Neo-Tethyan ocean. The selected Neo-Tethyan suites in Richards and Şengör (2017)
are from Cenozoic continental collision-related magmas, which cannot reflect the
oxidation state during Neo-Tethyan oceanic subduction. We recalculated the V/Sc
ratios for the pre-collisional Neo-Tethyan Mesozoic suites and found low V/Sc ratios
(median=6.9, n=786), contrasting with the high V/Sc ratios from Richards and Şengör
(2017), validating our independent redox constraints by zircon oxybarometry (Fig. 2d).

Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s acknowledgment of our comprehensive data
compilation. While our work confirms key principles linking magmatic oxidation to
porphyry Cu fertility, it advances the field in three novel ways, addressing unresolved

Prior studies (e.g., Richards and Şengör, 2017; Sillitoe, 2010) established broad

oxygen fugacity.

sulfides, enabling large-scale mineralization.

## Abstract

The Tethyan orogenic belt hosts numerous world-class porphyry copper deposits, with most forming during the Cenozoic continental collision and fewer during earlier Mesozoic subduction. To understand this pattern, we integrate redox indicators from detrital zircon grains with constraints from sedimentary geology and granite geochemistry during these times. Our analysis reveals a major shift from reduced magmas forming during the Mesozoic to more oxidized intrusive systems in the Cenozoic. Here we show that subduction of organic-rich, reduced marine sediments in the Mesozoic suppressed the oxidation state of arc magmas, locking chalcophile elements in the lower crust and inhibiting the formation of porphyry Cu deposits. In contrast, the subduction of more oxidized continental sediments during Cenozoic collision elevated the mantle’s oxidation state, releasing stored copper to melts that form porphyry deposits. These findings highlight the critical role of redox state of subducted sediments and tectonic history in shaping the distribution of porphyry mineralization along the Tethyan belt.

---

## Introduction

The Tethyan orogenic belt, extending for 12,000 km from the Pyrenees through the Alps and the Turkish–Iranian plateau, across Pakistan and the Himalayan–Tibetan Plateau, and into the Indochina Peninsula (Fig. 1a), is one of the world’s most important porphyry Cu belts1–4. This orogen formed through successive stages of continental breakup, ocean basin formation, and eventual collision between Gondwana-derived continents and Eurasia (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Material). The Tethys realm can be divided chronologically into the Proto-, Paleo-, and Neo-Tethys oceans, formed during the Early Paleozoic, Late Paleozoic, and Mesozoic, respectively5. Of particular interest is the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which opened in the Early Permian and underwent protracted subduction during the Mesozoic, culminating in extensive Cenozoic continental collisions that led to the formation of porphyry Cu deposits in regions such as the Gangdese and Yulong belts (Tibet), the Kerman belt (Iran), and the Anatolides belt (Turkey)1,2,5–8 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Material).

Despite a long Mesozoic subduction history, significantly fewer and smaller porphyry Cu deposits formed during subduction-related magmatism than during Cenozoic collisional or post-collisional magmatic stages in the Tethyan belt (Figs. 1b, 2c). The reason for this disparity remains elusive. A key control on porphyry copper formation is the oxidation state of the magmatic system, i.e., magmatic oxygen fugacity, commonly expressed as ΔFMQ (the log of oxygen fugacity relative to the fayalite–magnetite–quartz buffer). Oxidized arc magmas (ΔFMQ ≈ +1 to +2) favor the mobilization of chalcophile elements, enabling their transport to the upper crust9,10. Detrital zircon provides a valuable record of magmatic redox conditions over geologic timescales. Global geological events–particularly oceanic anoxic events and seawater incursion events–can influence the geochemical composition of subducted sediments11,12, altering mantle wedge oxygen fugacity and affecting porphyry mineralization potential.

Here, we apply a multidisciplinary approach to track the oxygen fugacity evolution of Tethyan magmas from the Early Jurassic to the Miocene. Using the novel zircon oxybarometer, we reconstruct ΔFMQ through time and integrate these data with sedimentary rocks, global sea-level and temperature changes, whole-rock geochemical data, and the timing of major geological events. Our findings illuminate the mechanisms responsible for redox variations in the mantle wedge and their implications for subduction- vs. collision-related porphyry Cu deposits.

---

## Results

Redox variation from Mesozoic to Cenozoic
Detrital zircon oxybarometry reveals an overall increase in ΔFMQ from the Early Jurassic through the Miocene in the Tethyan belt (Fig. 2d). Although data density during the Jurassic to Early Cretaceous is relatively low and thus more variable, Mesozoic ΔFMQ values are predominantly below +1. By contrast, Cenozoic ΔFMQ values commonly exceed +1, consistent with a transition to more oxidized magmatic conditions (Fig. 2d). The V/Sc ratios are also widely used as a redox proxy in igneous rocks, with higher ratios indicating more oxidized magmas19. The oxidation states of mid-oceanic ridge basalts (MORBs) close to ΔFMQ ~ 0 have V/Sc ratios of 6.74 ± 1.11. We compiled V/Sc data from Tethyan magmatic rocks (Supplementary Data 3). The results shows the lower V/Sc ratios of Mesozoic rocks (median = 6.9, n = 631) are like MORBs, while the Cenozoic rocks have higher V/Sc ratios (median = 8.4, n = 786) (Supplementary Fig. 2). The V/Sc results are consistent with our zircon ΔFMQ results, both indicated the Cenozoic ƒO2 is higher than the Mesozoic. Under low ƒO2, sulfur tends to form sulfides. The chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Au) have high partition coefficients between sulfide and silicate melts10. As a result, the chalcophile elements were sequestered in the lower crust via sulfide accumulation under low ƒO2, resulting in rare mineralization in the upper crust9,10,20. This process parallels the anoxic conditions inferred for the Paleo-Tethys Ocean basin during the Permian when the basin was in a restricted environment near the equator21,22. The correlation between redox state and porphyry Cu deposit frequency (Fig. 2c, d) supports redox-driven control over the spatiotemporal distribution of Tethyan porphyry Cu mineralization.

---

## Methods

Materials
The zircon age and trace elements are compiled from the global detrital zircon database68 and our newly acquired data in Tibet. The complete database includes 13981 detrital zircons (see details in Supplementary Data 2).

Zircon U–Pb dating and trace element analyses
Zircon grains were separated from two rivers in Tibet and mounted in epoxy resin for age and trace element determinations. Zircon U–Pb dating and trace element analyses were conducted simultaneously by laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA–ICP–MS) in the Mineral and Fluid Inclusion Microanalysis Laboratory, Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing, China. The NWR193UC laser ablation system (Elemental Scientific Lasers, USA) was equipped with a Coherent Excistar 200 excimer laser and a two-volume ablation cell. The laser ablation system was coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP–MS instrument (Agilent, USA). Zircons were mounted in epoxy resin discs, polished to expose grain interiors, cleaned ultrasonically in ultrapure water, and then cleaned again before analysis using analytical-grade methanol. Pre-ablation was conducted before each spot analysis using five laser shots (~0.3 μm in depth) to remove potential surface contamination. The analyses used a 30 μm laser beam diameter with a laser frequency of 8 Hz and fluence of 2 J/cm2. The Iolite software package was used for data reduction69. Zircons 91500 and GJ-1 were the primary and secondary reference materials, respectively. The exponential function was used to correct for down-hole fractionation70. NIST 610 and 91Zr were used to calibrate the trace element concentrations as an external reference material and internal standard, respectively. Zircon age and trace element data are listed in Supplementary Data 2.

Calculation of oxygen fugacity
Data points outside the Tethys domain were excluded. Zircon ages younger than 200 Ma are used for the following discussion to minimize the influence of the Paleo-Tethys Oceanic subduction because the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean occurred in the Late Permian–Late Triassic5. Zircons with a Th/U ratio of <0.1 were used to exclude metamorphic zircon71. Moreover, zircons derived from S-type granites were screened out using zircon P and REE contents72. After screening, 3010 zircon grains were used for reconstructing the Tethyan oxygen fugacity variation (Supplementary Data 2). The novel magmatic oxybarometer using ratios of Ce, U, and Ti in zircon is independent of temperature and pressure, with a standard error of ±0.6 log unit ƒO2 73. The ΔFMQ values can be calculated by the equation:

ΔFMQ = 3.998 (±0.124) × log[Ce / (U × T)] + 2.284 (±0.101) (1)

where Ui denotes age-corrected initial U content73. The ΔFMQ values are plotted as binned averages (bin size = 5 Myr).

Monte Carlo isotopic simulation
The Sr-Nd concentrations and isotopic ratios of the sediment–depleted mantle mixture can be calculated using the following equations:

Cx = Cs × F + Cm × (1 − F) (2)

Rx = Rs × F × Cs / Cx + Rm × (1 − F) × Cm / Cx (3)

where x is Sr or Nd, Cx, Cs, and Cm are element concentrations of x after mixing, sediment, and depleted mantle, respectively. Rx, Rs, and Rm are isotopic ratios of x after mixing, sediment, and depleted mantle, respectively, and F is the proportion of sediment-derived melt.

To obtain as many as possible mixture scenarios, random two pelagic or terrigenous sediments were selected and mixed to create a new pelagic or terrigenous sediment end-member. Then the new sediment end-member was mixed with the depleted mantle in random proportions. 30,000 pelagic sediment–mantle mixtures and 30,000 terrigenous sediment–mantle mixtures were generated using this method. The simulation results are shown in Fig. 4c, d.

Data availability
The data that support the findings of this study are available at Figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28424204).

## Paper

## Abstract

The Tethyan orogenic belt hosts numerous world-class porphyry copper deposits, with most forming during the Cenozoic continental collision and fewer during earlier Mesozoic subduction. To understand this pattern, we integrate redox indicators from detrital zircon grains with constraints from sedimentary geology and granite geochemistry during these times. Our analysis reveals a major shift from reduced magmas forming during the Mesozoic to more oxidized intrusive systems in the Cenozoic. Here we show that subduction of organic-rich, reduced marine sediments in the Mesozoic suppressed the oxidation state of arc magmas, locking chalcophile elements in the lower crust and inhibiting the formation of porphyry Cu deposits. In contrast, the subduction of more oxidized continental sediments during Cenozoic collision elevated the mantle’s oxidation state, releasing stored copper to melts that form porphyry deposits. These findings highlight the critical role of redox state of subducted sediments and tectonic history in shaping the distribution of porphyry mineralization along the Tethyan belt.

---

## Introduction

The Tethyan orogenic belt, extending for 12,000 km from the Pyrenees through the Alps and the Turkish–Iranian plateau, across Pakistan and the Himalayan–Tibetan Plateau, and into the Indochina Peninsula (Fig. 1a), is one of the world’s most important porphyry Cu belts1–4. This orogen formed through successive stages of continental breakup, ocean basin formation, and eventual collision between Gondwana-derived continents and Eurasia (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Material). The Tethys realm can be divided chronologically into the Proto-, Paleo-, and Neo-Tethys oceans, formed during the Early Paleozoic, Late Paleozoic, and Mesozoic, respectively5. Of particular interest is the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which opened in the Early Permian and underwent protracted subduction during the Mesozoic, culminating in extensive Cenozoic continental collisions that led to the formation of porphyry Cu deposits in regions such as the Gangdese and Yulong belts (Tibet), the Kerman belt (Iran), and the Anatolides belt (Turkey)1,2,5–8 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Material).

Despite a long Mesozoic subduction history, significantly fewer and smaller porphyry Cu deposits formed during subduction-related magmatism than during Cenozoic collisional or post-collisional magmatic stages in the Tethyan belt (Figs. 1b, 2c). The reason for this disparity remains elusive. A key control on porphyry copper formation is the oxidation state of the magmatic system, i.e., magmatic oxygen fugacity, commonly expressed as ΔFMQ (the log of oxygen fugacity relative to the fayalite–magnetite–quartz buffer). Oxidized arc magmas (ΔFMQ ≈ +1 to +2) favor the mobilization of chalcophile elements, enabling their transport to the upper crust9,10. Detrital zircon provides a valuable record of magmatic redox conditions over geologic timescales. Global geological events–particularly oceanic anoxic events and seawater incursion events–can influence the geochemical composition of subducted sediments11,12, altering mantle wedge oxygen fugacity and affecting porphyry mineralization potential.

Here, we apply a multidisciplinary approach to track the oxygen fugacity evolution of Tethyan magmas from the Early Jurassic to the Miocene. Using the novel zircon oxybarometer, we reconstruct ΔFMQ through time and integrate these data with sedimentary rocks, global sea-level and temperature changes, whole-rock geochemical data, and the timing of major geological events. Our findings illuminate the mechanisms responsible for redox variations in the mantle wedge and their implications for subduction- vs. collision-related porphyry Cu deposits.

---

## Results

Redox variation from Mesozoic to Cenozoic
Detrital zircon oxybarometry reveals an overall increase in ΔFMQ from the Early Jurassic through the Miocene in the Tethyan belt (Fig. 2d). Although data density during the Jurassic to Early Cretaceous is relatively low and thus more variable, Mesozoic ΔFMQ values are predominantly below +1. By contrast, Cenozoic ΔFMQ values commonly exceed +1, consistent with a transition to more oxidized magmatic conditions (Fig. 2d). The V/Sc ratios are also widely used as a redox proxy in igneous rocks, with higher ratios indicating more oxidized magmas19. The oxidation states of mid-oceanic ridge basalts (MORBs) close to ΔFMQ ~ 0 have V/Sc ratios of 6.74 ± 1.11. We compiled V/Sc data from Tethyan magmatic rocks (Supplementary Data 3). The results shows the lower V/Sc ratios of Mesozoic rocks (median = 6.9, n = 631) are like MORBs, while the Cenozoic rocks have higher V/Sc ratios (median = 8.4, n = 786) (Supplementary Fig. 2). The V/Sc results are consistent with our zircon ΔFMQ results, both indicated the Cenozoic ƒO2 is higher than the Mesozoic. Under low ƒO2, sulfur tends to form sulfides. The chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Au) have high partition coefficients between sulfide and silicate melts10. As a result, the chalcophile elements were sequestered in the lower crust via sulfide accumulation under low ƒO2, resulting in rare mineralization in the upper crust9,10,20. This process parallels the anoxic conditions inferred for the Paleo-Tethys Ocean basin during the Permian when the basin was in a restricted environment near the equator21,22. The correlation between redox state and porphyry Cu deposit frequency (Fig. 2c, d) supports redox-driven control over the spatiotemporal distribution of Tethyan porphyry Cu mineralization.

---

## Methods

Materials
The zircon age and trace elements are compiled from the global detrital zircon database68 and our newly acquired data in Tibet. The complete database includes 13981 detrital zircons (see details in Supplementary Data 2).

Zircon U–Pb dating and trace element analyses
Zircon grains were separated from two rivers in Tibet and mounted in epoxy resin for age and trace element determinations. Zircon U–Pb dating and trace element analyses were conducted simultaneously by laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA–ICP–MS) in the Mineral and Fluid Inclusion Microanalysis Laboratory, Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing, China. The NWR193UC laser ablation system (Elemental Scientific Lasers, USA) was equipped with a Coherent Excistar 200 excimer laser and a two-volume ablation cell. The laser ablation system was coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP–MS instrument (Agilent, USA). Zircons were mounted in epoxy resin discs, polished to expose grain interiors, cleaned ultrasonically in ultrapure water, and then cleaned again before analysis using analytical-grade methanol. Pre-ablation was conducted before each spot analysis using five laser shots (~0.3 μm in depth) to remove potential surface contamination. The analyses used a 30 μm laser beam diameter with a laser frequency of 8 Hz and fluence of 2 J/cm2. The Iolite software package was used for data reduction69. Zircons 91500 and GJ-1 were the primary and secondary reference materials, respectively. The exponential function was used to correct for down-hole fractionation70. NIST 610 and 91Zr were used to calibrate the trace element concentrations as an external reference material and internal standard, respectively. Zircon age and trace element data are listed in Supplementary Data 2.

Calculation of oxygen fugacity
Data points outside the Tethys domain were excluded. Zircon ages younger than 200 Ma are used for the following discussion to minimize the influence of the Paleo-Tethys Oceanic subduction because the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean occurred in the Late Permian–Late Triassic5. Zircons with a Th/U ratio of <0.1 were used to exclude metamorphic zircon71. Moreover, zircons derived from S-type granites were screened out using zircon P and REE contents72. After screening, 3010 zircon grains were used for reconstructing the Tethyan oxygen fugacity variation (Supplementary Data 2). The novel magmatic oxybarometer using ratios of Ce, U, and Ti in zircon is independent of temperature and pressure, with a standard error of ±0.6 log unit ƒO2 73. The ΔFMQ values can be calculated by the equation:

ΔFMQ = 3.998 (±0.124) × log[Ce / (U × T)] + 2.284 (±0.101) (1)

where Ui denotes age-corrected initial U content73. The ΔFMQ values are plotted as binned averages (bin size = 5 Myr).

Monte Carlo isotopic simulation
The Sr-Nd concentrations and isotopic ratios of the sediment–depleted mantle mixture can be calculated using the following equations:

Cx = Cs × F + Cm × (1 − F) (2)

Rx = Rs × F × Cs / Cx + Rm × (1 − F) × Cm / Cx (3)

where x is Sr or Nd, Cx, Cs, and Cm are element concentrations of x after mixing, sediment, and depleted mantle, respectively. Rx, Rs, and Rm are isotopic ratios of x after mixing, sediment, and depleted mantle, respectively, and F is the proportion of sediment-derived melt.

To obtain as many as possible mixture scenarios, random two pelagic or terrigenous sediments were selected and mixed to create a new pelagic or terrigenous sediment end-member. Then the new sediment end-member was mixed with the depleted mantle in random proportions. 30,000 pelagic sediment–mantle mixtures and 30,000 terrigenous sediment–mantle mixtures were generated using this method. The simulation results are shown in Fig. 4c, d.

Data availability
The data that support the findings of this study are available at Figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28424204).

## Paper

## Abstract

The Tethyan orogenic belt hosts numerous world-class porphyry copper deposits, with most forming during the Cenozoic continental collision and fewer during earlier Mesozoic subduction. To understand this pattern, we integrate redox indicators from detrital zircon grains with constraints from sedimentary geology and granite geochemistry during these times. Our analysis reveals a major shift from reduced magmas forming during the Mesozoic to more oxidized intrusive systems in the Cenozoic. Here we show that subduction of organic-rich, reduced marine sediments in the Mesozoic suppressed the oxidation state of arc magmas, locking chalcophile elements in the lower crust and inhibiting the formation of porphyry Cu deposits. In contrast, the subduction of more oxidized continental sediments during Cenozoic collision elevated the mantle’s oxidation state, releasing stored copper to melts that form porphyry deposits. These findings highlight the critical role of redox state of subducted sediments and tectonic history in shaping the distribution of porphyry mineralization along the Tethyan belt.

---

## Introduction

The Tethyan orogenic belt, extending for 12,000 km from the Pyrenees through the Alps and the Turkish–Iranian plateau, across Pakistan and the Himalayan–Tibetan Plateau, and into the Indochina Peninsula (Fig. 1a), is one of the world’s most important porphyry Cu belts1–4. This orogen formed through successive stages of continental breakup, ocean basin formation, and eventual collision between Gondwana-derived continents and Eurasia (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Material). The Tethys realm can be divided chronologically into the Proto-, Paleo-, and Neo-Tethys oceans, formed during the Early Paleozoic, Late Paleozoic, and Mesozoic, respectively5. Of particular interest is the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which opened in the Early Permian and underwent protracted subduction during the Mesozoic, culminating in extensive Cenozoic continental collisions that led to the formation of porphyry Cu deposits in regions such as the Gangdese and Yulong belts (Tibet), the Kerman belt (Iran), and the Anatolides belt (Turkey)1,2,5–8 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Material).

Despite a long Mesozoic subduction history, significantly fewer and smaller porphyry Cu deposits formed during subduction-related magmatism than during Cenozoic collisional or post-collisional magmatic stages in the Tethyan belt (Figs. 1b, 2c). The reason for this disparity remains elusive. A key control on porphyry copper formation is the oxidation state of the magmatic system, i.e., magmatic oxygen fugacity, commonly expressed as ΔFMQ (the log of oxygen fugacity relative to the fayalite–magnetite–quartz buffer). Oxidized arc magmas (ΔFMQ ≈ +1 to +2) favor the mobilization of chalcophile elements, enabling their transport to the upper crust9,10. Detrital zircon provides a valuable record of magmatic redox conditions over geologic timescales. Global geological events–particularly oceanic anoxic events and seawater incursion events–can influence the geochemical composition of subducted sediments11,12, altering mantle wedge oxygen fugacity and affecting porphyry mineralization potential.

Here, we apply a multidisciplinary approach to track the oxygen fugacity evolution of Tethyan magmas from the Early Jurassic to the Miocene. Using the novel zircon oxybarometer, we reconstruct ΔFMQ through time and integrate these data with sedimentary rocks, global sea-level and temperature changes, whole-rock geochemical data, and the timing of major geological events. Our findings illuminate the mechanisms responsible for redox variations in the mantle wedge and their implications for subduction- vs. collision-related porphyry Cu deposits.

---

## Results

Redox variation from Mesozoic to Cenozoic
Detrital zircon oxybarometry reveals an overall increase in ΔFMQ from the Early Jurassic through the Miocene in the Tethyan belt (Fig. 2d). Although data density during the Jurassic to Early Cretaceous is relatively low and thus more variable, Mesozoic ΔFMQ values are predominantly below +1. By contrast, Cenozoic ΔFMQ values commonly exceed +1, consistent with a transition to more oxidized magmatic conditions (Fig. 2d). The V/Sc ratios are also widely used as a redox proxy in igneous rocks, with higher ratios indicating more oxidized magmas19. The oxidation states of mid-oceanic ridge basalts (MORBs) close to ΔFMQ ~ 0 have V/Sc ratios of 6.74 ± 1.11. We compiled V/Sc data from Tethyan magmatic rocks (Supplementary Data 3). The results shows the lower V/Sc ratios of Mesozoic rocks (median = 6.9, n = 631) are like MORBs, while the Cenozoic rocks have higher V/Sc ratios (median = 8.4, n = 786) (Supplementary Fig. 2). The V/Sc results are consistent with our zircon ΔFMQ results, both indicated the Cenozoic ƒO2 is higher than the Mesozoic. Under low ƒO2, sulfur tends to form sulfides. The chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Au) have high partition coefficients between sulfide and silicate melts10. As a result, the chalcophile elements were sequestered in the lower crust via sulfide accumulation under low ƒO2, resulting in rare mineralization in the upper crust9,10,20. This process parallels the anoxic conditions inferred for the Paleo-Tethys Ocean basin during the Permian when the basin was in a restricted environment near the equator21,22. The correlation between redox state and porphyry Cu deposit frequency (Fig. 2c, d) supports redox-driven control over the spatiotemporal distribution of Tethyan porphyry Cu mineralization.

---

## Methods

Materials
The zircon age and trace elements are compiled from the global detrital zircon database68 and our newly acquired data in Tibet. The complete database includes 13981 detrital zircons (see details in Supplementary Data 2).

Zircon U–Pb dating and trace element analyses
Zircon grains were separated from two rivers in Tibet and mounted in epoxy resin for age and trace element determinations. Zircon U–Pb dating and trace element analyses were conducted simultaneously by laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA–ICP–MS) in the Mineral and Fluid Inclusion Microanalysis Laboratory, Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing, China. The NWR193UC laser ablation system (Elemental Scientific Lasers, USA) was equipped with a Coherent Excistar 200 excimer laser and a two-volume ablation cell. The laser ablation system was coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP–MS instrument (Agilent, USA). Zircons were mounted in epoxy resin discs, polished to expose grain interiors, cleaned ultrasonically in ultrapure water, and then cleaned again before analysis using analytical-grade methanol. Pre-ablation was conducted before each spot analysis using five laser shots (~0.3 μm in depth) to remove potential surface contamination. The analyses used a 30 μm laser beam diameter with a laser frequency of 8 Hz and fluence of 2 J/cm2. The Iolite software package was used for data reduction69. Zircons 91500 and GJ-1 were the primary and secondary reference materials, respectively. The exponential function was used to correct for down-hole fractionation70. NIST 610 and 91Zr were used to calibrate the trace element concentrations as an external reference material and internal standard, respectively. Zircon age and trace element data are listed in Supplementary Data 2.

Calculation of oxygen fugacity
Data points outside the Tethys domain were excluded. Zircon ages younger than 200 Ma are used for the following discussion to minimize the influence of the Paleo-Tethys Oceanic subduction because the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean occurred in the Late Permian–Late Triassic5. Zircons with a Th/U ratio of <0.1 were used to exclude metamorphic zircon71. Moreover, zircons derived from S-type granites were screened out using zircon P and REE contents72. After screening, 3010 zircon grains were used for reconstructing the Tethyan oxygen fugacity variation (Supplementary Data 2). The novel magmatic oxybarometer using ratios of Ce, U, and Ti in zircon is independent of temperature and pressure, with a standard error of ±0.6 log unit ƒO2 73. The ΔFMQ values can be calculated by the equation:

ΔFMQ = 3.998 (±0.124) × log[Ce / (U × T)] + 2.284 (±0.101) (1)

where Ui denotes age-corrected initial U content73. The ΔFMQ values are plotted as binned averages (bin size = 5 Myr).

Monte Carlo isotopic simulation
The Sr-Nd concentrations and isotopic ratios of the sediment–depleted mantle mixture can be calculated using the following equations:

Cx = Cs × F + Cm × (1 − F) (2)

Rx = Rs × F × Cs / Cx + Rm × (1 − F) × Cm / Cx (3)

where x is Sr or Nd, Cx, Cs, and Cm are element concentrations of x after mixing, sediment, and depleted mantle, respectively. Rx, Rs, and Rm are isotopic ratios of x after mixing, sediment, and depleted mantle, respectively, and F is the proportion of sediment-derived melt.

To obtain as many as possible mixture scenarios, random two pelagic or terrigenous sediments were selected and mixed to create a new pelagic or terrigenous sediment end-member. Then the new sediment end-member was mixed with the depleted mantle in random proportions. 30,000 pelagic sediment–mantle mixtures and 30,000 terrigenous sediment–mantle mixtures were generated using this method. The simulation results are shown in Fig. 4c, d.

Data availability
The data that support the findings of this study are available at Figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28424204).

Response to Reviewer #2
This manuscript reads well. It is a good compilation of a large amount of data that
confirms the paper published in Geology by Richards and Sengor, 2017. Richards and
Sengor showed that very few porphyry copper deposits formed during the Paleo-
Tethyan subduction due to organic-rich sediments subducted to the mantle, and that
large deposits formed during later Neo-Tethyan subduction. This manuscript provides
the compilation of data related to the oxidation conditions of magmas using the well-
established method based on zircon trace-element composition, to confirm the shift in
oxidation conditions of igneous rocks, which reflects the source mantle.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comparison of our work to Richards & Şengör
(2017), and we acknowledge their foundational contributions to understanding Paleo-
Tethyan anoxia and its impact on magma fertility. However, our work is distinct from
Richards and Şengör (2017) in several ways:
(i) Scope of Study: Richards and Şengör (2017) focused on the sparsity of porphyry
copper deposits associated with Paleo-Tethyan (Permian to Jurassic) ocean subduction,
whereas our work focuses on the Neo-Tethyan (Cretaceous-Cenozoic) ocean
subduction. The Paleo-Tethys and Neo-Tethys oceans are completely different entities.
(ii) Findings: Richards and Şengör (2017) emphasized that most porphyry copper
deposits in the Tethyan belt formed during subduction of the Neo-Tethyan ocean basin
in the late Mesozoic–Cenozoic due to high magmatic oxidation states. Our findings are
opposite; we identified that most porphyry deposits in the Tethyan belt are associated
with Cenozoic continental collision, while fewer are formed during subduction of the
Neo-Tethyan ocean. The selected Neo-Tethyan suites in Richards and Şengör (2017)
are from Cenozoic continental collision-related magmas, which cannot reflect the
oxidation state during Neo-Tethyan oceanic subduction. We recalculated the V/Sc
ratios for the pre-collisional Neo-Tethyan Mesozoic suites and found low V/Sc ratios
(median=6.9, n=786), contrasting with the high V/Sc ratios from Richards and Şengör
(2017), validating our independent redox constraints by zircon oxybarometry (Fig. 2d).
This manuscript compiles types of sediments, the location and size of porphyry copper
deposits, and data of host igneous rocks (Supplementary text and data). In this sense,
this manuscript provides a useful compilation of data from many porphyry copper
deposits along the Tethyan subduction zone. As mentioned, the data compilation
confirms the conclusion of Richards and Sengor, that there was a change in the
oxidation conditions of the mantle and in the resultant magmas. The manuscript also
confirms other earlier publications, that oxidized magmas are conducive for porphyry
copper mineralization (e.g., Sillitoe, 2010; Shen et al., 2015; Loucks et al., 2024), and
that subducted sediments influence the oxidation conditions of the mantle and magmas
(e.g., Wang et al., 2007; Evans, 2012),
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s acknowledgment of our comprehensive data
compilation. While our work confirms key principles linking magmatic oxidation to
porphyry Cu fertility, it advances the field in three novel ways, addressing unresolved
questions and introducing new methodologies:
Prior studies (e.g., Richards and Şengör, 2017; Sillitoe, 2010) established broad
correlations between oxidation state and mineralization. However, our detrital zircon
ΔFMQ (Fig. 2d) provides the first quantitative record of redox evolution across the
Tethyan belt. We found a transition from a reduced environment during Mesozoic
oceanic subduction (ΔFMQ < +1) to an oxidized environment during Cenozoic
continental collision (ΔFMQ > +1), which has not been previously constrained. By
correlating zircon ΔFMQ with stratigraphic records of organic-rich vs. carbonate
sediments (Fig. 3), we demonstrate that sediment composition directly modulates
mantle redox.
The earlier works focused on single qualitative parameters (e.g., whole-rock V/Sc ratio),
our study integrates diverse quantitative and qualitative proxies to trace the variation of
oxygen fugacity.
A key unresolved issue in Richards and Şengör (2017) was how Neo-Tethyan Mesozoic
barren magmas relate to Cenozoic mineralization. Our two-stage model (Fig. 5)
addresses this: Reduced magmas sequestered Cu in lower-crustal sulfides during the
Mesozoic and increase of oxygen fugacity during the Cenozoic remobilized these
sulfides, enabling large-scale mineralization.
The authors stress formation of large porphyry copper deposits during continental
collision; the Neo-Tethys plate and overlying sediments were subducted long after the
closure of the Neo-Tethys, resulting in mantle metasomatization. The continental
collision and closure of the sea does not mean the end of subduction of oceanic plate.
This has been well illustrated by many tomographic images of subducted slabs below
the Asian continent. Therefore, emphasizing the collision stage for large porphyry
copper deposits is misleading and confuses the issue.
Response: We agree that the Neo-Tethys oceanic plate and overlying sediments would
subduct long after the closure of the Neo-Tethys Ocean. The continental collision-
related porphyry deposits in our manuscript mainly refer to post-collisional porphyry
deposits. For example, the Gangdese porphyry Cu deposits mainly formed in the
Miocene, which is about 40~45 Myr later than the initial collision between Indian and
Asian continents (~55–60 Ma). The breakoff of the oceanic plate happened in ~45 Ma
(Zhu et al., 2022). Thus, it is unlikely the post-collision porphyry mineralization is
related to the mantle metasomatism by the Neo-Tethys oceanic slab. Instead, the mantle
is more likely metasomatized by the subducted continental plate. We intended to
emphasize that the composition of subducted sediments changed fundamentally from
oceanic subduction to the post-collisional stage, which directly drove mantle oxidation
and porphyry Cu formation.
The manuscript has stratigraphic columns of sediments, to provide support for the
authors’ proposal, but the sections are essentially similar to Figure 3 of the paper by
Richards and Sengor. During the Mesozoic, sediments were reduced, such that their
subduction led to the mantle being reduced, resulting in the formation of reduced
magmas.
Response: We appreciate this comment. However, our stratigraphic columns differ
from Figure 3 of Richards and Şengör (2007), which is evident in the ages of these
columns. For example, Figure 3 of Richards and Şengör (2007) covers Carboniferous
to Triassic stratigraphic columns from the Paleo-Tethyan Ocean basin. In contrast, our
Figure 3 provides representative stratigraphic columns from Jurassic to Neogene for the
Neo-Tethys. Additionally, our stratigraphic columns are located on the passive
continental margins to the south of the Neo-Tethys Ocean (Fig. S1C). Therefore, the
northward subduction of these sediments is most likely to influence the mantle source
beneath the Tethyan Cu belt. Consequently, our stratigraphic columns support the
sediment-driven oxidation variation.
Response to Reviewer #3
Overall, this paper is well-written and presents a compelling narrative. The authors have
compiled a comprehensive dataset encompassing porphyry deposits, sedimentary rocks,
global sea-level and temperature fluctuations, whole-rock geochemistry, and major
geological events. Their analysis reveals a strong correlation between redox variations
and key geological events in the Tethyan domain. Furthermore, they highlight the
critical role of subducted sediment composition in modulating redox conditions and
controlling porphyry Cu deposit formation. Given the novelty and significance of these
findings, I believe this manuscript is well-suited for Nature Communications. I
recommend minor revisions and suggest a few points that could further strengthen the
manuscript during the revision process:
1. Lines 173–174: The authors state that as mantle-derived ultrapotassic magmas
ascend from ~56 km to ~15 km depth, their ΔFMQ increases from +0.8 to +3.0, yet
their ability to significantly oxidize magma in the lower crust remains limited. However,
in Lines 50–51, they also mention that oxidized arc magmas (ΔFMQ ≈ +1 to +2) promote the mobilization of chalcophile elements, facilitating their transport to the upper crust. Considering the uncertainties in oxygen fugacity calculations, FMQ +0.8
is nearly equivalent to FMQ +1. Additionally, oxygen fugacity estimations from detrital
zircons inherently carry errors. The authors could cite more recent references, as the
oxygen fugacity of porphyry-related magmas is generally considered to be higher in the
deep source with high pressure.

lower crust (ΔFMQ ≈ +0.8) is limited. See revised texts in new Lines 185–189.
